title: TorQ
oneLine: A tracked garage robot that listens, answers car-repair questions out loud with Claude, and keeps its safety logic off the network.

specs.Role: The software: Claude tool loop, speech in and out, body service, drive firmware, dashboard and tests

intake.question: What is it, in one sentence?
intake.hint: Plain description of the thing, not the pitch.
intake.draft: A tracked shop robot that stores service manuals and puts the right page on a screen in its belly, so every number arrives with its source next to it.

intake.question: Role, timeline, status
intake.hint: What you did on it, over what period, and where it stands now.
intake.draft: Solo concept and design, now a group build. Twelve weeks, September to December 2026. In progress: design locked, parts not yet ordered.

intake.question: What made it hard?
intake.hint: The real constraint: budget, tooling, physics, time, a dependency you did not control.
intake.draft: The first version was a small tracked robot that decided whether an item was trash, compost or recycling, picked it up and put it in its belly. The classification was the fun part and it would have come together fast. The problem is that the robot only exists if it can pick the item up, and household waste is the worst case for grasping: a crushed can, a peel, a film wrapper and a bottle all need different grasps and none of their shapes are known in advance. Realistic payload at our budget is 50 to 150g, less than a full drink can. So the impressive half was the easy half, and the risk all sat at the end of the schedule.

intake.question: What did you decide, and what did you reject?
intake.hint: One decision where you chose the harder correct route over the quick one.
intake.draft: I moved the project into a domain I already work in, and swapped the hard problem from handling things to knowing things. The option I rejected was keeping the sorting robot and scoping it down, to place items by hand rather than have it find them. I rejected it because at that point the person is already holding the item and could just put it in the bin, so the version that saves anyone anything is the version that is much harder. Swapping the job removed the arm, the gripper and the inverse kinematics in one move, taking the design from nine moving joints to four.

intake.question: What number can you put on it?
intake.draft: Nothing measured yet, the build has not started. Candidates once it runs: lookup latency, offline hit rate against a manual, or battery life under load. Design figures that exist now are 4 servos and a 495 dollar parts list, but neither is measured.

intake.question: What broke, and what did you do?
intake.draft: Nothing yet, the build has not started.

intake.question: What media do you have?
intake.draft: None yet. First real images will be the bench rig in week 3 and the head assembly on the desk in week 4.

intake.question: What would you do differently?
intake.hint: Two sentences. A design judgement, not self criticism.

intro: TorQ is a small tracked robot for a home garage. You ask it a question while your hands are on a wrench, like "what's the lug nut torque on my Civic?", and it answers through a speaker. It remembers which vehicle you are working on and keeps job notes. You can also drive it from a browser dashboard.

The part I want an AI/ML reader to look at is the voice assistant. I built it end to end: speech in, a streaming tool-use loop written directly against the Anthropic SDK, and speech out. It is a work in progress. This page uses present tense only for what exists in the repo, and everything else sits under "What is next".

The screenshot at the top is the real dashboard and the answers in it are real Claude answers. The robot was offline when I captured it, so the body code was running on my laptop against the simulated drive controller from the test suite. Photos and video of the robot itself are still to come.

sections.label: Architecture
sections.title: A body and a brain
body: The robot is split in two on purpose. Anything slow or expensive, meaning the speech models and the language model, runs on the laptop. Anything that has to keep working when the network drops, meaning stopping the motors, runs on the robot.

flow.summary: Three computers in a chain. A Mac, the brain, runs the brain server, Whisper speech-to-text, the Claude tool loop, Piper text-to-speech, job memory and the browser dashboard. It talks over a WebSocket, carrying JSON and binary audio frames in both directions, to a Raspberry Pi 5, the body, which runs motor control with clamps and trim, microphone capture, speaker playback, telemetry and the camera stream. The Pi talks over USB serial, in both directions, to an Arduino Uno with a motor shield running the drive firmware: a 300 ms watchdog, a latched E-stop, an overcurrent cutoff, ramping and active braking.

sections.label: LLM loop
sections.title: How the AI part works
body: The loop is written directly against the Anthropic SDK, with no agent framework. Each question is routed first. Everyday questions go to Claude Haiku 5.5 at low effort, for speed. Questions that look diagnostic, containing words like "why", "noise", "leak" or "misfire", go to Claude Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort.

The model has four tools: get_vehicle_info, set_vehicle, save_note and stop. Every tool input is validated in code before anything runs. A bad input goes back to the model as an error result instead of executing. The loop is capped at 6 tool rounds per question.

Reply text streams from the model into a sentence chunker. Each complete sentence is synthesized and sent to the robot while the model is still writing the rest, so the robot starts talking before the answer is finished. A new question, or the Quiet button, cancels the answer in flight and the audio already queued on the robot.

flow.summary: One question, start to finish. A question arrives by push-to-talk or typed. Whisper transcribes it on the laptop. A router picks Haiku or Sonnet. Claude streams a turn, and if it calls a tool the input is validated, the tool runs and the result goes back, for up to 6 rounds. Reply text goes through a sentence chunker, each sentence is synthesized by Piper, and the audio plays on the speaker on the Pi.

boxes.title: Question
boxes.note: Hold T on the dashboard to talk, or type it.

boxes.title: Transcribe
boxes.note: faster-whisper (small.en), local on the laptop, primed with shop vocabulary.

boxes.title: Route
boxes.note: Haiku at low effort, or Sonnet at medium effort for diagnosis.

boxes.title: Claude, streaming
boxes.note: System prompt, tool definitions and the growing conversation are all cached.

stages.aside: Tool call? Validate the input, run it, send the result back. Up to 6 rounds.

boxes.title: Sentence chunker
boxes.note: Waits for a whole sentence, then hands it on.

stages.label: one sentence at a time

boxes.title: Speak
boxes.note: Piper text-to-speech on the laptop, played on the speaker on the Pi.

stages.aside: A new question or Quiet cancels everything queued.

after: The system prompt is written for speech: no markdown, units spelled out ("eighty foot-pounds"), answer first. It tells the model to say so plainly when it is not confident in a number, and to point to the service manual.

Failure handling is written for a voice interface. Every API failure, whether a bad key, a rate limit, no network, a refusal or a truncated tool call, maps to a short sentence TorQ can say aloud. The user is never left with silence.
Prompt caching covers the system prompt, the tool definitions and the growing conversation. The system prompt is frozen and the tool order is fixed, so the cached prefix stays valid.

sections.label: Safety
sections.title: Safety does not depend on the model
body: A runaway robot breaks ankles, so stopping is handled in three independent layers. The language model sits at the top of the stack and the lower layers do not trust it. The model's only motor tool is stop.
sections.callout: The model can stop the robot. It cannot drive it.

head: Layer
Where it runs
What it enforces
rows: Stops the motors if a drive command is not repeated within 300 ms. Latched E-stop. Current-sense cutoff at 1.9 A sustained for 300 ms. Speed ramping and active braking.
Speed clamps and a command timeout, so a bad command from anywhere upstream cannot exceed them.
Driving is hold-to-drive. Closing the dashboard tab stops the robot. An E-stop locks out all driving until it is explicitly reset.

images.alt: The Drive, Robot and Events panels of the dashboard during manual driving. The W and D keys are lit, the Manual button reads "Manual: on", and Motor PWM reads L 144 R 101. The Pi address reads 127.0.0.1 and the CPU temp, Supply and Wi-Fi rows are blank. The event log shows "manual override ON".

sections.label: Numbers
sections.title: Why the model is not trusted with numbers
body: A wrong torque spec strips a thread or loses a wheel. Today TorQ answers from the model's own knowledge, so the current build handles that risk with prompting: hedge, and point to the manual. You can see it working in the screenshot, where the lug nut answer ends with "Confirm it in the owner's manual before you finish."
That is a prompt, not a guarantee, and I do not claim the problem is solved. The planned build handles it structurally, with retrieval and citations. It is described under "What is next".

sections.label: Pivot
sections.title: The project I dropped first
body: The project began as a robot that collects and composts trash. I dropped it for reasons I could state. Hot composting needs roughly a cubic yard of material to sustain its own heat, which a small robot cannot carry. One compost cycle takes 4 to 8 weeks, which leaves almost no room to iterate. And collection depends on grasping, which is where hobby robots usually fail.
TorQ inverts each of these. The hard part is knowing things, the feedback loop is one second, and a half-finished TorQ is still a useful rolling screen.
The line from my notes: "Don't build a robot that solves a problem you'd have to research. Build one that solves a problem you have."

sections.label: Bench
sections.title: What went wrong on the bench
body: On the first bench test the left track ran slower than the right. The motor shield's current-sense pins showed the left motor drawing about 1.5 to 2 times the current of the right at the same PWM, and stalling at 30% power. That pointed at mechanical drag and away from software. The cause turned out to be a stripped gearbox in the left motor. A replacement motor is the next hardware task.

Loud replies made the USB speaker brown out and reset on battery power, which showed up in the kernel log as USB disconnects. The fix for now is a software volume cap that is re-applied before every reply. A separate 5 V supply is the real fix and is on the list.

sections.label: Next
sections.title: What is next
body: None of this section is built yet. Today TorQ answers from the model's own knowledge and is prompted to hedge. Cited service-manual lookup is what will replace that hedge with a page you can read. It is the feature the project is ultimately for.

The design: service-manual PDFs will be ingested on the laptop into per-page images and embeddings. Pages will be retrieved locally on the robot, and the page itself will be shown next to any answer. Online, Claude will answer from the retrieved pages using the API's native citations, which return the page number as a structured field. Offline, the robot will fall back to a spec table extracted at ingest time.

The governing rule will be that TorQ never shows a number without showing where it came from, so a wrong answer is visible instead of silent. The design docs are docs/CONCEPT.md and docs/LLM.md in the repo.

sections.label: Tests
sections.title: Tests, and where the code is
body: There are 20 integration tests and all of them pass. They run the real brain server and the real body code over real sockets, against a simulated Arduino that speaks the firmware's serial protocol, plus stand-ins for Claude, Whisper and Piper.

They cover the behaviours that matter. The watchdog stops the motors when the brain disappears. E-stop locks out driving. Invalid tool input is reported and not run. A new question interrupts the current answer. A missing API key produces a spoken explanation instead of a crash.

imagePrompt: a small boxy tracked robot with a compact cube shaped body riding on black rubber treads, having no arms at all and no limbs of any kind. On a short jointed neck it carries a binocular head built from two large cylindrical eyes set side by side: the left eye is a camera lens with visible glass elements, the right eye is a lamp with a clear reflector, switched on. A hinged flat display panel folds down out of a bay in the front of the body and tilts up toward the viewer, its screen a blank flat grey. Weathered matte machined aluminium and black plastic, workshop worn. Standing on a concrete floor with a workbench and a few hand tools out of focus behind it.

proposalArchived.audience: Written for the group. Read it, then tell me what you think.
summary: I want us to build TorQ instead of the sorting robot. Ask it a torque spec and it finds the page in our service manuals, then displays it on a hinged screen in its belly, tilted up to your eyeline. It is also a lit inspection magnifier for reading part numbers, it films your teardown with its own light, it picks up dropped fasteners with a magnet, and it runs timers for torque sequences and cure times.

The chassis, drive, power, compute and sensors are the same robot we already planned. What changes is what it carries and what it does with it. This is a payload swap, not a restart, and roughly 70 percent of the build is untouched.

sections.label: Mechanism
sections.title: How it works
sections.callout: The governing rule: it never shows a value without showing where the value came from. A wrong torque figure damages an engine or loses a wheel, so the job is not to know the answer, it is to find the page and put it on screen so you can check it yourself.

pipelines.label: Phase 1, on a laptop, once per manual
steps: PDF, render every page to PNG (pymupdf)
sqlite: manual, page, text, embedding, png
optional vision pass, structured torque rows
copy the folder to the robot
pipelines.note: This runs on a real computer, never on the Pi. OCR and embedding a 400 page scan is slow and nobody is waiting on it. The optional vision pass is where a model is safest: it extracts tables we can check once against the page and then trust, instead of improvising a number live.

pipelines.label: Phase 2, on the robot, per question
steps: question, typed on your phone, tapped, or spoken
embed the query locally on the Pi
top k pages by similarity, filtered by vehicle
SHOW THE PAGE IMAGE on the belly
if online: a model reads those pages and returns plain English plus a structured citation
if offline: hit the pre extracted spec table, instant, no model
pipelines.note: The citation is not prose the model writes and we hope is honest. The API returns the page number as a structured field, so we render that page next to the answer and a wrong answer becomes visible rather than silent.

head: State
What you get
rows: Plain English answer and the cited manual page
Pre extracted spec table and the page image. Faster than online
The retrieved page, you read it yourself
Still a mobile display you can drive around

after: There is no single point of failure anywhere in that ladder. That is the property the compost robot never had.

sections.label: Hardware
sections.title: Four moving joints, total
body: Two brains, on purpose. A Raspberry Pi 5 runs the screen, web app, camera, retrieval and model calls. An RP2350 holds a 200Hz control loop, the servo bus, motor PID, encoders, the cliff watchdog and the e stop. They talk over USB serial at about 50Hz.

Linux cannot hold a real time loop. The microcontroller keeps the robot safe, stopping at cliffs and cutting the motors, even if the Pi reboots, hangs, or we crash it while developing. That is what stops a bug from becoming a robot on the floor.

columns.label: Drive, 2 motors
items: 2 N20 gearmotors at 1:100 with magnetic encoders, TB6612FNG driver, closed loop velocity PID on the MCU
Printed sprockets, idlers and road wheels, TPU track pads
3 VL53L1X time of flight sensors: one forward, two down at the track nose so it cannot drive off a bench
Encoders are not optional. Without them it cannot drive straight

columns.label: Head, 3 servos
items: Pan, neck tilt, head tilt
Pi Camera Module 3 Wide with autofocus, for filming, the magnifier, part numbers and VIN plates
A COB LED ring coaxial with the lens, so it lights exactly what the camera sees and aiming the head aims both
2 GC9A01 round LCDs for eyes, with Perlin idle motion and variable blink so it does not read as broken when still

columns.label: Belly, 1 servo
items: 7 inch DSI touchscreen on a spring counterbalanced hinge
Tilts to your eyeline. Floor and bench need very different angles, and a fixed screen is unreadable half the time
The counterbalance matters: without it the servo holds screen weight all day, heats up and drains the pack

columns.label: Senses, no motors
items: BNO085 IMU, which detects being picked up and doubles as a digital angle gauge for driveline work
INMP441 mic mounted high away from motor whine, plus a rubber push to talk button, because shops are loud
MAX98357A amp and a 5W speaker. Buy the good one: chirps forgive a cheap driver, speech does not
Magnets: a parts tray on the top deck, and a removable sled underneath that sweeps up dropped screws as it drives

after: Power is where these builds die. A 2S2P 18650 pack at about 25Wh, with separate rails: 5V at 5A for the Pi, 6V for the servo bus, common ground, fat bulk caps. Servo inrush browning out the Pi is the number one killer of Raspberry Pi robots. Get it wrong and we spend the term chasing mystery reboots through a closed chassis.

Head pan, neck tilt, head tilt, belly hinge. No arms, no gripper, no legs. Earlier versions of this design had nine joints. Every one we deleted is a bracket, a wire, a tuning session and a failure mode we do not spend the term on.

after: Track C is the important one. It is the whole product, it is the riskiest software, and it needs no hardware at all, so somebody can start it on day one while the rest of us wait on shipping. If it fails we find out in week 2 with ten weeks to recover, instead of week 9 with none.
A and B converge at week 7 for integration. C and D converge at week 9 on the belly.

sections.label: Delivery
sections.title: What ships, even if things go wrong

tiers.title: A rolling screen that shows you the right page
tiers.body: Drives, will not fall off a bench, tilts its screen, finds the manual page, magnifies a part number, picks up dropped screws, runs timers. No voice, no video, no language model, and still a real tool, three weeks before the deadline.

tiers.title: Plain English answers with cited pages
tiers.body: Ask in your own words, get the number and the exact page it was read off. Roughly four dollars a month to run.

tiers.title: Voice, then video
tiers.body: Hands free control for when your hands are covered in oil, and how tos on the belly. Separate bets, so losing either breaks nothing underneath it.

tiers.title: Codes, angles and a personality
tiers.body: OBD-II trouble codes chained straight to the manual diagnostic page. A digital angle gauge for driveline work. Reading specs aloud. The idle behaviours that make it feel like something rather than a cart.

after: If we fall behind we cut in this order, decided now while we are calm: video search, then photo log, then voice, then the motorized hinge, then the model. Never the manual search or the screen.

Parts come to about 495 dollars core, 552 with a spares kit. Order in week 1, all at once, because servo lead times run 2 to 4 weeks, which is a quarter of our project spent waiting if we are slow. Four things I would not cut at any price: separate power rails, motor encoders, cliff sensors, and the spares kit. Those are what stand between us and a project that dies in week six.

closing.label: Where I stand
closing.lead: I am attached to this one. I have put the work in because I think it is the right call for us, and I would rather say that straight than pretend I am neutral about it.
body: It is still our project, though, so if you do not like it I am not asking you to just go along with it.

bar.intro: Bring an alternative worked out to the same level:
items: What hardware it needs, down to a parts list and a budget
What software it needs, and which part is the hardest
A 12 week schedule with the risky work scheduled early
Where it fails, and what still ships when it does
bar.outro: Put that on the table and if it is better than this, I will build yours. What I would rather we did not do is pick something on the strength of the idea alone and find out in week eight that the hard part was never going to land. That is what would have happened with the sorting robot, and the only reason it costs us nothing is that we worked it out in week zero.

capabilities.intro: Here is the whole range, because the reason I want this one is that a single small machine covers all of it. Every line below runs on the same four servos, one camera with a light ring, one screen, one microphone and one magnet. Nothing here needs a part we are not already buying.

items.lead: Torque specs, with the page on screen
items.note: Ask for the lug nut torque on a 2015 Civic and get the number with the actual manual page under it. It never shows a value without its source.

items.lead: Ask in your own words
items.note: Not a search box. Say what you are doing and it works out the vehicle and the fastener.

items.lead: Wiring diagrams and exploded views
items.note: Same library, different query. Free once the manuals are ingested.

items.lead: Fluid capacities and fill specs
items.note: How much goes in, what grade, where the plug is.

items.lead: Torque sequences that count with you
items.note: Shows the criss cross pattern and tracks bolt 3 of 10 so you do not lose your place.

items.lead: A spec table you can edit
items.note: The figures you look up constantly get saved locally, so they are instant and they work with no internet at all.

items.lead: The light and the camera point the same way
items.note: The LED ring is coaxial with the lens, on a head that aims both at once. You cannot film a teardown properly on a phone because one hand is already holding the flashlight. This is the whole reason it can film in an engine bay.

items.lead: Mark a step by voice while your hands are busy
items.note: Say mark and it bookmarks that moment in the recording. No stopping, no clean hands required.

items.lead: Plays the steps back in reverse for reassembly
items.note: Taking something apart and not remembering how it goes back together is the universal one. It hands you your own bookmarks, backwards.

items.lead: Photo per step as the cheap version
items.note: Say photo, it timestamps into a job log and builds a reverse order gallery. Works even if we never finish video.

items.lead: Timelapse of a whole job
items.note: Set it on the bench and let it run. The camera is already there and already lit.

items.lead: Before and after, side by side
items.note: Shoot the assembly intact, shoot it apart, compare the two on the belly.

items.lead: Footage you can actually post
items.note: Lit, steady, from a fixed angle that is not your elbow. Teardown videos worth putting somewhere.

items.lead: A lit inspection magnifier
items.note: Camera and ring light on the belly screen, for casting numbers and date stamps in a dark bay. Probably the thing we reach for most.

items.lead: Remote eyes under the car
items.note: Drive it where your head does not fit and watch on your phone while you steer the head.

items.lead: Reads a part number and looks it up
items.note: Point it at a casting number, it reads the text and searches the manuals for it.

items.lead: Reads a VIN and filters everything to that car
items.note: Scan the door jamb and every lookup after that is narrowed to the right vehicle and year.

items.lead: Pulls trouble codes and opens the right page
items.note: A fifteen dollar Bluetooth dongle to the OBD port, then the code goes straight to the diagnostic tree in the manual. 1996 and newer.

items.lead: Live data on the belly
items.note: Coolant temp, RPM, fuel trims and O2 sensors while it idles.

items.lead: Freeze frame and code clearing
items.note: Capture the conditions when the fault set, then clear it once you have fixed it.

items.lead: A digital angle gauge
items.note: Set it on a surface and read the angle. Driveline and pinion angles, checking a lift is level, corner ride heights. That is a sixty dollar tool.

items.lead: Gauges drawn at exact scale on the glass
items.note: Thread pitch gauge, bolt diameter chart, a ruler. Hold the fastener against the screen.

items.lead: Unit conversion and timers
items.note: Foot pounds to newton metres, cure times, brake bleed cycles, oil drains.

items.lead: Magnets that pick up what you drop
items.note: A tray on top you can throw bolts into without bending down, and a sled underneath that sweeps the floor as it drives.

items.lead: Send it to sweep the floor
items.note: Say sweep and it patterns across the shop collecting dropped hardware, then brings it back.

items.lead: Records a noise so you can compare it
items.note: Capture a knock or a squeal at different revs, keep it, play it back next week or send it to someone.

items.lead: Voice control
items.note: Pause, back thirty, next step, without touching anything. Plus a rubber button you can hit with a knuckle when the shop is loud.

items.lead: Reads the spec out loud
items.note: For when you are under the car and cannot see the screen. It says the number and names the source, never just the number.

items.lead: How to videos on its belly
items.note: Cached, so they keep playing when the shop WiFi drops.

items.lead: Your phone is the same interface
items.note: The belly and your phone run one web app. Type the awkward stuff on the phone, read it off the robot.

items.lead: Voice notes
items.note: Say note, need a new gasket, and it is written down and attached to the job.

items.lead: It comes to you and angles the screen
items.note: Drives over, turns to face you, and tilts the display up so you can read it from the floor.

items.lead: A log per vehicle
items.note: What you did, when, at what mileage, with the photos from that job attached.

items.lead: Add manuals whenever you want
items.note: Drop in a new PDF, it gets ingested once, and it is searchable forever after.

items.lead: A folder for new abilities
items.note: Anything we write later drops into a skills folder and shows up on the belly. It does not need rebuilding to learn something.

items.lead: It behaves like something, not a cart
items.note: Animated eyes, idle head motion, and it reacts when you pick it up or tilt it.

items.lead: It notices when you are stuck
items.note: Ten minutes on the same bolt and it offers the spec without being asked.

items.lead: It watches what you are working on
items.note: Head follows your hands, light already pointed where you need it.

capabilities.caveat: That is thirty odd things, and no, not all of it lands in twelve weeks. I am listing the full range because it is all reachable on this one set of parts, which is the argument. The floor we have to hit by week 9 is the manual lookup, the magnifier, the magnets and the timers, with no voice and no model at all. Filming and voice are week 10. The rest is what the hardware already affords once that exists, and any of it can be added later without touching the robot.

origin.label: Why I am moving off the last idea
origin.title: The sorting robot, and why this one is better
was: The original was a small tracked robot that looked at an item, decided whether it was trash, compost or recycling, picked it up and put it in its belly. It never composted anything. It was a sorting robot with a bin, and the interesting part was the deciding.

I still think the classification is a good idea. A camera and a small model can tell a can from a banana peel from a plastic wrapper, and watching a robot make that call and act on it is a genuinely good demo.
origin.liked: So this is not me deciding the idea was stupid. It is me working out that the part that makes it work is not the part that makes it look good, and that we would not have found that out until late.

problems.lead: Picking things up was the whole product, and it is the hardest thing on the list
problems.note: Deciding what an item is does not do anything on its own. The robot only exists if it can pick the item up, and household waste is the worst case for that: a crushed can, a banana peel, a film wrapper and a bottle each need a different grasp, and none of their shapes are known in advance. That is a research problem, not a twelve week problem.

problems.lead: The easy half is the half that looks impressive, so the risk sits at the end
problems.note: Classification would have come together fast and looked great. The manipulation is where it dies. That means the project feels like it is going well right up until the point where there is no time left to change course. That risk profile is the one I most want to avoid.

problems.lead: A drink can weighs more than it can lift
problems.note: Realistic payload at our budget is 50 to 150g. A full can is several times that. Even a working gripper would have handled a subset of household waste small enough that it would not have been useful.
Once the battery, the compute and the drive are in, a robot this size has maybe a litre or two of space left. That is a couple of items before a human has to come and empty it.

problems.lead: If a person has to be standing there, it has not saved anyone anything
problems.note: You were already holding the item. You could have put it in the bin. The version that actually helps is the one that finds things across a room on its own, which needs navigation and search on top of the grasping. The useful version is much harder than the demo version.

problems.lead: Being mostly right about recycling is worse than not sorting
problems.note: What is recyclable depends on your municipality and your hauler, and it changes. One wrong item can contaminate a whole load. That is a rule set we do not control and cannot verify, attached to a failure that is invisible to us.
If the gripper does not work we have a camera that names your rubbish. There is no partial version of that robot that is worth having, which is the property a hard deadline punishes most.

origin.verdict: TorQ inverts the risk. The essential part, finding the right page and putting it on screen, is a laptop program we can build in week 2 before a single part arrives, so if it is going to fail it fails while we still have ten weeks. And when something does go wrong it degrades into something useful instead of into nothing: no model, still a manual page; no retrieval, still a screen on wheels you can drive. The belly even survived the change. It still opens, it just holds a display instead of a bin.
